text: Sensitive and confidential sound like synonyms for 'protect this,' but they protect against two different kinds of harm. This lesson draws that line, because Chapter 2's classification labels have to account for both.

Sensitive data is data that harms the person it describes if it's exposed: health records, biometric data, sexual orientation, religious beliefs, financial account numbers. The harm is personal, embarrassment, discrimination, fraud, even physical danger. Confidential data is a different category entirely: information an organization protects for business reasons, independent of any personal harm. Trade secrets, unreleased merger plans, proprietary source code, internal financial statements before they're public. If a competitor gets your unreleased roadmap, nobody's privacy was violated, but the business damage can be severe.

These categories overlap, but they aren't identical. A health record is sensitive but usually isn't confidential, the company isn't protecting its own trade secret. An unreleased merger plan is confidential but isn't sensitive, no individual's health or orientation is at stake. And some data is genuinely both: an executive's salary and health benefits file is sensitive to that person and confidential to the company that doesn't want compensation structures public.

This distinction matters because classification labels, public, internal, confidential, and restricted, have to account for both kinds of risk at once. A scheme that only thinks about business confidentiality will under-protect a customer's health data. A scheme that only thinks about personal sensitivity will under-protect the company's unreleased financials.
Sensitive protects the person; confidential protects the business; some data needs both. Next up: data classification concepts, where this groundwork turns into actual labels.
